openingProblem.problem: Franco ruled Spain for 36 years and chose his own successor. Within seven years of his death Spain had a democratic constitution, had defeated a military coup, and had elected a Socialist government. How did a dictatorship turn into a democracy without revolution?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: who made the Spanish transition?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Franco's Spain, 1939–1975
chunks.body:
General Francisco Franco staged a military coup in 1936 and, after victory in the Civil War, ruled Spain unchallenged from 1939 until his death in 1975. Independent political parties were banned, and until 1967 Spain had no constitution at all. The regime rested on the army, which was rewarded and celebrated, and on the Catholic Church, which under a 1953 concordat was freed from taxation and given the right to demand censorship. Everything distinctively Basque was repressed, and in 1958 the Basque separatist organisation **ETA** was formed to fight for independence; in December 1973 it assassinated Franco's prime minister, Admiral Carrero Blanco.

Yet Spain changed beneath the dictatorship. In 1959 a group of technocratic ministers abandoned two decades of economic self-sufficiency for a **Stabilization Plan**. Spain joined the IMF and the World Bank, and GNP rose steadily from 1961. One worker in two had been on the land in 1950; by 1971 it was one in five. Millions of tourists arrived: 34 million in the year before Franco's death. Judt warns against overstating this "economic miracle", much of which depended on emigrants' remittances and foreign holiday-makers. But by the late 1960s strikes and demonstrations were a fixture of Spanish life, and an unofficial labour movement had grown in Catalonia and the Basque country.

As Judt puts it, it was the political state, not Spanish society, that had fallen behind. Franco named the young **Juan Carlos**, grandson of Spain's last king, as his successor. A US intelligence assessment of May 1975 judged that the regime "must change in order to survive but any real change carries threats to its existence".

This mattered because society had modernised while politics had not, which meant that by 1975 there was a large gap between the regime and the people it ruled.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Franco's regime rested on the army and the Church.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: By the end it depended on passive acceptance.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Society had outgrown the regime by 1975.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Economic change under Franco prepared the ground for democracy without intending to.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The 1959 Stabilization Plan opened Spain to the world economy; by 1971 only one worker in five was on the land, and 34 million tourists visited in the year before Franco's death.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that daily life and expectations changed far more than the regime, so, as Judt argues, the political state rather than society had fallen behind.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt warns that the 'miracle' depended heavily on emigrants' remittances and foreign tourists, and income per head in 1973 was less than half the EEC average.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Economic change therefore created a society ready for democracy, but not the democracy itself.

chunks.title: Transition from above, 1975–1978
chunks.body:
Franco died on **20 November 1975**. Judt stresses that the transition was managed from inside the ranks of Franco's own ministers and appointees, which helps explain its speed and success. King **Juan Carlos** at first kept Franco's last prime minister to reassure the army, but in 1976 replaced him with **Adolfo Suárez**, a 44-year-old official who had headed Franco's own National Movement. Judt compares Suárez to Gorbachev: a product of the system he dismantled.

Suárez moved fast. He persuaded the Francoist assembly to accept a referendum on political reform, introducing universal suffrage and a two-chamber parliament, which passed on **15 December 1976** with over 94 per cent in favour. In 1977 he legalised the Socialists (PSOE) of Felipe González, the trade unions and, a week after dismantling the National Movement, the Communist Party. The **June 1977 elections**, the first since 1936, gave Suárez's UCD 165 seats and the Socialists 121; without a majority, Suárez had to work with the left.

The parties also cooperated on the economy. Inflation had reached 26 per cent a year, and in October 1977 the **Moncloa Pacts** between politicians, unions and employers agreed devaluation, an incomes policy and spending controls. They "worked no miracles", Judt writes, but without them divisions would have been worse. The **Constitution** of December 1978, confirmed by referendum, made Spain a parliamentary monarchy with no official religion, lowered the voting age to eighteen, abolished the death penalty and gave the historic regions a right to autonomy.

This mattered because democracy was built through negotiation between reformers from the old regime and the former opposition, which meant that the transition avoided both revolution and a conservative backlash.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The left soon played a central role.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Legalising all parties made democracy genuine.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Communists' legalisation angered the army.

chunks.title: Threats to democracy, 1978–1982
chunks.body:
Democracy faced two serious threats. The first was **ETA**. A Basque Statute of Autonomy was approved by referendum in 1979, but ETA, demanding full independence, stepped up its campaign and killed 181 people in 1979–80. By 1982 Spain was on its way to becoming seventeen self-governing regions, while Madrid kept defence, justice and foreign affairs.

The second threat came from the army. In January 1981 Suárez resigned, forced out by his own party. On **23 February 1981** Lieutenant Colonel Antonio **Tejero** of the Civil Guard seized the Cortes at gunpoint, and General Milans del Bosch declared a state of emergency in Valencia, calling on the king to install a military government. **King Juan Carlos** refused and defended the Constitution in a televised speech. The coup collapsed. Those nostalgic for Franco turned instead to Manuel Fraga's Popular Alliance, within the law. Afterwards the Cortes cut the military budget and legalised divorce.

In **October 1982** the Socialists won an absolute majority, and Felipe González became prime minister. The UCD was reduced to two seats. Power had passed peacefully to a party that had been illegal six years earlier.

This mattered because the defeat of the coup discredited military intervention, which meant that the 1982 Socialist victory could take place without fear of the army.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It showed how fragile democracy still was.

chunks.title: Consolidation and its costs, 1982–2000
chunks.body:
Felipe González governed Spain for fourteen years. The Socialists had promised to protect jobs and take Spain out of NATO. In power González did the opposite: he kept austerity, modernised and later privatised industry, and in **1986** won a referendum in favour of staying in NATO. In his view Spain's future lay "not in socialism but in Europe". On **1 January 1986** Spain joined the European Community, receiving regional subsidies and doing well out of membership.

There was a darker side. From 1983 to 1987 counter-terrorist squads, the **GAL**, operated illegally from France and killed twenty-six ETA operatives with the government's approval. When journalists revealed this "dirty war" in the mid-1990s, together with graft by Socialist ministers, the scandals ended González's career. Judt notes that they aroused anxiety about the moral condition of "a Spanish democracy still in its infancy".

Yet the system worked. On 3 March 1996, amid recession, high unemployment and the scandals, the Socialists lost a general election for the first time since 1979. José María Aznar's People's Party formed a minority government with the support of Catalan, Basque and Canarian nationalists, ending more than thirteen years of Socialist rule. Judt calls the democratic transitions of southern Europe "quite the most remarkable and unexpected development of the age".

This mattered because power passed peacefully between left and right and Spain was anchored in Europe, which meant that by 2000 democracy was consolidated even though its record contained abuses.

argumentsThatWork.claim: González anchored Spain in the West and Europe.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt calls it a moderate response in the circumstances.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1996 election showed democracy was consolidated.

useItInAnEssay.judge: González therefore consolidated democracy's institutions while damaging trust in its leaders.

modelPlan.thesis: The 1978 Constitution addressed regional demands by granting the historic regions a right to autonomy, leading to seventeen self-governing regions and a Basque statute; but it kept defence, justice and foreign affairs in Madrid, which ETA and Basque nationalists rejected.
modelPlan.counter: ETA killed 181 people in 1979–80 despite the Basque statute.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How far did autonomy solve the problem? For most regions; not for ETA.

segments.text: The 1978 Constitution addressed regional problems by turning Spain into a state of autonomous regions.
It gave the historic regions a right to autonomy; a Basque Statute of Autonomy was approved in 1979, and Spain was divided into seventeen self-administering regions.
This meant that regional identities repressed under Franco were recognised within a democratic state, so most regional parties worked within the system.
However, Madrid kept defence, justice and foreign affairs, and ETA, demanding full independence, killed 181 people in 1979–80.
The constitution therefore solved the regional question for most Spaniards, but not for those who wanted independence.

essayQuestions.text: To what extent did Felipe González's governments consolidate democracy in Spain between 1982 and 1996?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far

modelPlan.thesis: González's governments consolidated democracy by anchoring Spain in NATO and the European Community and governing from the centre, but the GAL dirty war and corruption damaged trust, and his party's peaceful defeat in 1996 completed the consolidation.
modelPlan.counter: Judt notes the scandals aroused anxiety about the moral condition of a young democracy.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Consolidated by what measure? Institutions and alternation, yes; integrity, no.

segments.text: González's governments consolidated Spanish democracy, despite serious abuses.
He won the 1986 NATO referendum, Spain joined the EC on 1 January 1986, and his party governed from the centre for fourteen years.
This meant that Spain's democracy was anchored in Western institutions, so a return to dictatorship became unthinkable.
However, the GAL killed twenty-six ETA operatives in 1983–87 with government approval, and the mid-1990s revelations, with corruption scandals, ended his career.
Democracy was therefore consolidated, as the Socialists' peaceful defeat in March 1996 showed, even though its leaders had abused it.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the threat posed by the armed forces to democracy in Spain and Argentina between 1981 and 1990.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The threat from the armed forces
decodeKey.judgement: How serious was each threat, and how was it overcome?

modelPlan.thesis: Both democracies faced military revolts that failed, but Spain's single coup attempt of 1981 was defeated outright by the king and followed by cuts to the military budget, whereas Argentina's repeated revolts of 1987–90 won concessions on justice before Menem crushed the last one and pardoned the officers.

arguments.claim: Similarity: revolts against the new democracy failed.
Difference: one defeat versus repeated revolts.
Difference: the role of the head of state.

modelPlan.counter: No revolt took power in either state, and in Argentina an estimated 200,000 people gathered to defend democracy in 1987.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which threat was greater? Argentina's, because its army forced concessions repeatedly.

segments.text: Military revolts threatened democracy in both Spain and Argentina, but Argentina's army extracted far more.

In Spain Tejero seized the Cortes on 23 February 1981 but King Juan Carlos defended the Constitution, whereas in Argentina Aldo Rico's revolt of April 1987 was followed by the Law of Due Obedience in June.
This meant that Spain's coup discredited military intervention, so the Cortes could then cut the military budget, while Argentina's revolts limited the prosecution of officers.
However, both threats ended in failure: Argentina's last revolt, in December 1990, was crushed within 36 hours, though Menem then pardoned the most important convicted officers.
The armed forces were therefore a weaker threat in Spain, where the monarchy held them in check, than in Argentina, where democracy survived only by giving ground on justice.
